hints: Look closely at the diagram of the slide. Because it is printed life-size, the size of the stem circle you can measure on the page is the real actual size of the specimen.
Remember what the x40 label should mean for a drawing. It should mean drawing size divided by actual specimen size, not just the microscope setting used.
walkthrough:
**Find the actual size of the specimen**

Think like a biologist. The question tells you the diagram is the same size as the actual slide, so you can measure the stem diameter directly from the diagram.

That measured value is the actual size, about a few millimetres. It is very small.

**Calculate the magnification of the drawing**

The magnification stated on a plan drawing must always be calculated from the drawing itself.

Key rule:
$$\text{magnification} = \frac{\text{image size (drawing size)}}{\text{actual size}}$$

Here image size is 20 cm. When you divide 20 cm by the tiny actual size, you get a value much bigger than 40.

**Compare to the x40 label**

The microscope was set to x40, but the student drew the stem at 20 cm diameter. That drawing is magnified more than 40 times compared to the real stem.

So labelling the plan as x40 is wrong because the drawing magnification is actually larger than x40.

options.A: An eyepiece graticule is useful for measuring, but you do not need it here because the diagram already gives you actual size life-size.
options.B: Actual size is a fixed property of the specimen and does not change with low or high power, only the magnified image size changes.
options.C: Correct. Drawing size of 20 cm divided by the very small actual size gives a magnification greater than x40, so the x40 label understates the drawing.
options.D: The opposite is true. Because the actual stem is so tiny, a 20 cm drawing represents more than a 40 times enlargement, not less.
